note: Restaurants, cafés, bakeries and eateries in BARMM, each seen operating in 2025–26 on its own Facebook page or in a Bangsamoro Government release, as of November 2026. Halal is marked only where a source says so ("certified" only with a named certifier); ask when you visit.

eats.name: Cheraf's Resto
eats.note: Restaurant and caterer listing itself as a halal restaurant; dishes such as beef randang; a second branch opened at KCC Mall of Cotabato in January 2026
eats.about: Cheraf's is a home-style restaurant on Pansacala Street that lists itself as a halal restaurant and cooks the dishes Cotabato families serve at home, such as beef randang, the Maranao and Maguindanaon cousin of Malaysian rendang, slow-cooked in spiced coconut. In January 2026 it opened a second counter, Cheraf's Kitchenette, on the second floor of KCC Mall of Cotabato. Much of its work is catering: weddings, aqiqah (the naming feast for a newborn), kanduli thanksgiving meals, corporate lunches and whole-day events, served buffet-style. It suits a quick local lunch in the city centre or anyone planning a halal spread for a gathering.
eats.why_go: For home-style Maguindanaon and Maranao dishes like beef randang from a kitchen that calls itself halal.
tips: Takes catering for weddings, aqiqah, kanduli, birthdays and corporate events
Accepts credit card payments

eats.name: Coffee Spot
eats.note: Open-air coffee shop under string lights; Italian-style coffee, pastries and snacks
eats.about: Coffee Spot is a roadside coffee shop beside the Husky Terminal on Sinsuat Avenue that sets out to bring Italian-style coffee to Cotabato City. Tables sit under string lights in an open-air setting, with an indoor room behind the bar; the menu runs from espresso drinks and matcha to cheesecake slices, fries and pasta. It keeps long hours, staying open late into the night, and during the last days of Ramadan it opens from evening until 2 AM for the after-tarawih crowd. A car wash in the same compound means you can have your car cleaned while you drink.
eats.why_go: For a late-night coffee and cheesecake on Sinsuat Avenue after most cafés have closed.
tips: Has run late hours (until 2 AM) on some nights and during Ramadan

eats.note: Bakeshop and restaurant (since 1985): cakes, breads and meals; also caters events
eats.about: Connie's is a bakeshop on Don Rufino Alonzo Street with a restaurant attached. It is best known for celebration cakes: layered dedication cakes, Black Forest, ube and fondant cakes decorated to order for birthdays and graduations. The dining room also hosts set-table dinners, and the shop takes catering inquiries. Come here to order a cake for an occasion or to pick up bread and pastries.

tips: Takes orders for dedication, graduation and wedding cakes

eats.name: Datu's Brew
eats.note: Coffee shop that roasts and sells its own coffee and muscovado sugar
eats.about: Datu's Brew in Rosary Heights X describes itself as a coffee shop that tells the story of its people: it displays fine handicrafts of Maguindanao and frames itself as a small part of peace-building in Mindanao. It sells its own freshly ground coffee and local muscovado sugar in packs, alongside brewed coffee, cakes and pastries such as blueberry cupcakes. After a quiet spell the page announced in 2026 that its coffee and muscovado were back, sold by message order in sizes and bundles. It suits visitors who want local coffee to take home and a café with a cultural angle.
eats.why_go: For locally packed ground coffee and muscovado sugar from a café rooted in Maguindanaon culture.

eats.address: Door 1, Sabal Building, corner Pascual Street, Sinsuat Avenue
eats.note: Pastry café and restaurant (est. 2022): macarons, cakes, chicken wings and coffee; also runs baking classes
eats.about: Golden Crust is a pastry café and restaurant at the corner of Pascual Street and Sinsuat Avenue, opened in 2022 and marking its 4th anniversary in November 2026. Its counter is built around baked goods: macarons, cheesecakes such as Bento burnt cheesecake, cookies, churros and banana pudding, plus savoury chicken wings in several sauces and coffee topped with its homemade cream. It runs baking classes and workshops, and launches limited items like its cloud cake by comment reservation. It suits a dessert-and-coffee stop or a box of pastries to bring to a visit.
eats.why_go: For macarons, cheesecakes and baked treats made in-house, plus baking workshops.
tips: Limited items are reserved by commenting MINE and the quantity on its posts

eats.name: Hala Bira Halal Food
eats.note: Halal eatery known for beef bulalo and papaitan
eats.about: Hala Bira Halal Food is a small eatery on Jose Lim Sr. Street that Cotabato City has known for years for two soups: beef bulalo, a clear broth of beef shank and marrow bone with corn and greens, and papaitan, a bitter, tangy beef tripe soup. It also serves fried dalag (mudfish) and home-style rice plates, and its name and page make a point of the food being halal. It opens early and closes mid-afternoon, so it is a breakfast and lunch place; delivery runs through local riders such as Maxim. A sister counter, HAB HUB, has opened on the De Mazenod side.
eats.why_go: For a steaming bowl of halal beef bulalo or papaitan, the dish locals send visitors to.
tips: Regular hours posted after Eid 2026: 6:00 AM – 3:30 PM

eats.about: Hello Cafe is the café of Cha Tuk Chak Cotabato, a milk-tea shop with a glass front at 21C Sinsuat Avenue, with a ground floor and a second floor for walk-in guests. Drinks run from Biscoff and pistachio milk teas to seasonal specials, and the kitchen adds burgers, pasta and seafood plates meant to be paired with them. It hosts family events such as a Halloween party for children, and is open daily for dine-in and takeout. It suits families and groups of friends looking for a bright, casual spot.

It serves iced matcha, coffee and cream drinks with comfort food such as loaded fries, onion rings, waffles and chicken, in a bright room with a few tables. eats.note: Café and restaurant (est. 2011): coffee, cakes, pasta and fried hito (catfish); a 2019 review called it halal-certified
eats.about: Jamaica Le Cafe is a café-restaurant on Level 2 of the Mall of Alnor on Sinsuat Avenue that travel writers were already recommending in 2018; a 2019 review in Edge Davao described it as halal-certified. Beyond cakes such as Mango Bravo and coffee, its kitchen serves Filipino and Asian plates, including fried hito (catfish) with spiced vinegar, crab rice and creamy shrimp pasta. The space also hosts community events such as a garage-sale weekend in November 2026. It suits a relaxed meal with dessert after shopping at the mall.
eats.why_go: For fried hito and a slice of Mango Bravo cake in one stop at the Mall of Alnor.

eats.name: Katto Koffee
eats.note: Small coffee bar serving matcha from Nishio and Uji, Japan, and espresso drinks
eats.about: Katto Koffee is a small coffee bar at the Katto Shophouse on Notre Dame Avenue, beside the PSA building, that bills itself as "good coffee only". Its focus is matcha from Nishio and Uji, the two Japanese regions best known for growing tea for matcha; it sources from makers such as Marukyu Koyamaen and introduces named matcha like Matsukaze, describing their tasting notes (umami, seaweed, white chocolate, nuts). Drinks include matcha and strawberry matcha lattes and seasonal coffees such as a pumpkin spice latte, and the owners occasionally share matcha they bring back from their travels. It suits matcha lovers and anyone wanting a quiet weekday stop near Notre Dame.
eats.why_go: For matcha from Nishio and Uji, Japan's best-known matcha regions, rare this far south.

eats.address: Sinsuat Avenue, Rosary Heights 4 (fronting NDRVM); branch on T.V. Juliano Street, Bagua 3
eats.note: Hito (catfish) and tilapia house
eats.about: La Hitopia is a grill and restaurant built around hito (catfish) and tilapia, its tagline a pun: "Fish be with yah". The main branch at the Tocao Residence on Sinsuat Avenue, fronting Notre Dame RVM, celebrated five years in September 2025, and a second branch faces Kutawato Cave on T.V. Juliano Street. Hito is usually fried crisp and eaten with spiced vinegar and rice, a favourite across Cotabato. The place is popular with teams and government offices for group meals and gives free cakes to graduates celebrating there.
eats.why_go: For fried hito and tilapia at a restaurant devoted to them.

It is registered with PhilGEPS, so it regularly supplies government offices and BARMM agencies with packed meals, snack boxes and themed food corners. Its spreads lean to yellow rice, chicken, fish, salads and fruit. It suits groups and offices that need halal food for an event in Cotabato City.
eats.why_go: For a dependable halal caterer that can feed an event or an office seminar.
tips: Caters weddings, nikah, aqeeqah and corporate events in Cotabato City and nearby

eats.name: Moro Grounds Restaurant
eats.note: Tausug and Moro dishes such as satti, tiyula itum and beef sinina; halal-certified by Maslaha Halal Certification Board Inc., July 2026 to July 2027
eats.about: Moro Grounds serves Moro cuisine, the cooking of the Tausug, Maguindanaon and Maranao, in Cotabato City, with a sister restaurant in Davao. In 2026 both branches were halal-certified by the Maslaha Halal Certification Board. Look for satti, Tausug grilled skewers served in a spicy, peanut-rich sauce with rice cakes, often eaten for breakfast; tiyula itum, a black beef soup coloured with burnt coconut; and beef sinina. It also hosts iftar during Ramadan and delivers large packed-meal orders around the region.
eats.why_go: For certified-halal satti and tiyula itum, the Tausug classics, in Cotabato City.
tips: Takes bulk packed-meal orders

eats.name: Pagana by the Bay
eats.note: Seafood restaurant on the water at Timako; opened in 2023 as Timako Bay Seafood Resto, a halal diner, and now run under the Pagana name
eats.about: Pagana by the Bay sits on the water at Timako in Kalanganan II, the hill and mangrove shore at the mouth of the Rio Grande where Cotabato City meets Illana Bay. It opened in 2023 as Timako Bay Seafood Resto, which the Bangsamoro Board of Investments described as a halal diner, and is now run by the Pagana group behind Pagana Kutawato. Its open deck faces west over the bay, so sunset is the time to come; it also hosts gatherings such as sunset yoga. The kitchen focuses on seafood and Maguindanaon dishes.
eats.why_go: For seafood with a sunset over Illana Bay from an open deck on the water.

eats.name: Pagana Kutawato Native Restaurant
eats.note: Maguindanaon native dishes and seafood on a pork-free menu, with function rooms for events; hosted a MAFAR activity in April 2026
eats.about: Pagana Kutawato, on Rufo Mañara Street in Rosary Heights 11, was established in 2011 and calls itself Cotabato City's first native restaurant; pagana is the Maguindanaon word for a feast laid out for guests. The menu is Maguindanaon cooking and fresh seafood without pork, served with brass bowls and gongs as part of the décor. It doubles as an events venue, with a VIP hall for about 20 people and the Sultan Hall for up to 80, and belongs to the same group as Cotabato Cubes Hotel and Pagana by the Bay. It suits visitors wanting a first taste of Maguindanaon food and groups needing a function room.
eats.why_go: For a sit-down Maguindanaon feast in the city's longest-running native restaurant.
tips: VIP Hall for about 20 guests and Sultan Hall for up to 80, bookable for meetings and events

eats.about: Tambayan sa Timako ("hangout on Timako") is a restaurant on Timako Hill in Kalanganan 2, the green headland above the mangroves at Cotabato City's seaward edge. Terraced swimming pools look out over the mangrove forest toward the mountains, and the indoor lounge has sofas and a counter. It has a mini function hall for gatherings such as aqiqah. eats.note: Malay restaurant: roti canai with curry, biryani and teh tarik
eats.about: TEAroti is a Malay restaurant on 1st Street at the MSU main campus, named for teh tarik and roti, the Malaysian pulled tea and flatbread. Regulars come for biryani, roti canai with curries, curry laksa, mee goreng and halo-halo. In Ramadan it opens from 3 PM to 11 PM and takes iftar bookings. It suits anyone missing Malaysian food or curious to try it.
eats.why_go: For roti canai, biryani and teh tarik on the MSU campus.
tips: In Ramadan: open daily 3:00 PM – 11:00 PM; iftar dine-ins and pick-ups can be booked from 2:00 PM; no deliveries

eats.name: House of Maguindanaon Delicacies
eats.note: Maker of Maguindanaon sweets such as bulua, tipas, dudul and putri mandi, sold by the box or tray
eats.about: House of Maguindanaon Delicacies (est. 2010) makes traditional Maguindanaon sweets by order for events like kanduli, weddings and aqiqah. The range includes bulua (sponge-like buns), tipas (crisp fried pastry), dudul (a sticky sweet of glutinous rice, coconut milk and sugar, also made with durian), putri mandi (coconut-filled rice balls), panganan sising (ring-shaped fritters) and panyalam (rice pancakes), packed in boxes, bilao and trays, and it sends orders as far as Surallah in South Cotabato. It suits visitors wanting pasalubong of Maguindanaon sweets.
eats.why_go: For boxed Maguindanaon sweets like dudul and tipas to take home.
tips: Customised boxes and trays on request; message for quotes
